description: We are enthusiastic engineering students passionate about technology, innovation, and problem-solving. Our interests include electronics, programming, AI, and developing creative solutions to real-world problems. We believe in teamwork, creativity, and continuous learning. We welcome passionate members who have skills in Python, C, web development, hardware, UI/UX design, and presentation. Let's collaborate, share ideas, and build something impactful together!
summary: Earth Trend Detective is a browser tool that helps students and the public find and test trends in NASA Earth science data. A short wizard suggests variables with plain-language definitions. In the Detective Lab, users load a demo or a time series from NASA Giovanni and get a plot, the rate of change, and significance tests (regression, Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope). It covers the challenge’s four goals: choosing variables, regional data, time-series visualisation and significance testing. Built-in GPM rainfall and SeaWiFS river examples show how real trends are read, and why “not significant” can simply mean more data is needed.
details:
Earth Trend Detective is a browser tool that helps students and the public investigate trends in NASA Earth science data. A short wizard suggests variables with plain-language definitions. In the Detective Lab, users load a demo or a time series from NASA Giovanni; the tool averages the data, can remove the seasonal cycle, plots it, and reports what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant, using linear regression with a 95% confidence interval, the Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope.

Benefits: no coding or installation, runs in any browser, data stays on the user's device, and results come with plain-language explanations and warnings when a record is too short or noisy.

Intended impact: to build trend literacy. Users learn that a trend needs enough data, that seasonal cycles are not trends, and that "not significant" can mean "needs more data".

Tools and technology: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with charts and statistics written by hand (no libraries), hosted on GitHub Pages and usable on any ordinary laptop or phone. NASA data used: GPM IMERG (rainfall demo), SeaWiFS chlorophyll (ten river-outflow case files) and GES DISC Giovanni (source for user uploads).

Creativity: a "detective" approach with a four-part answer (what, where, how much, significant?); a synthetic practice series with a known built-in trend so users can check the tests work; and a replay of a published river-chlorophyll study that shows how outliers change a slope.

Factors considered: short records and outliers, seasonal cycles, autocorrelation, privacy (nothing is uploaded), a beginner-friendly audience, and honest limits (only linear trends are tested, as the challenge suggests).
